Dominic Baldwin
CEO & Founder · Xentum

"The industry let my father down. Everything we do is a direct response to that."

Where it begins

My father's story

My father grew up on a farm in Cumbria. He was a practical man — good with his hands, proud of where he came from, and deeply trusting of the people around him. When he inherited a significant sum of money at a young age, he needed guidance. Not a sales pitch. Not someone working out how to maximise their own income from his situation. A genuine guide.

What he got was something quite different. A series of decisions made by people who were — at best — not thinking carefully enough about whose interests they were serving. Products that served the adviser more than the client. Complexity that didn't need to exist. Fees that weren't explained. The kind of advice that only reveals its true cost over years, not days.

When he died in 2004, I sat with the paperwork and began to understand what had happened. It hurt. Not just financially — though it did hurt financially — but in a deeper way. He was a decent, trusting man who didn't understand the industry he was dealing with. He had no framework for knowing what good advice looked like, what questions to ask, or when he was being failed.

"He didn't need a sales pitch and somebody only in the room to benefit themselves. He needed an honest, authentic guide — and to help him find one, he really needed an unbiased guide to financial advice."
Dominic Baldwin, Founder — Xentum

Read the Buyer's Guide to Financial Advice →

That experience is the reason Xentum exists. Not as a marketing story. As a structural commitment. Every decision we've made about how we charge, how we're owned, how we employ our advisers, and how we talk about our conflicts of interest flows directly from that afternoon in 2004 going through my father's files.

Who does what

The four roles in financial services — explained

Most people assume there's just "the adviser" and "the investment." In reality, up to four separate organisations are involved — each with a distinct role, a separate cost, and a different impact on your outcomes. Understanding this is one of the most important things you can do before choosing a firm.

Role 1
Financial Adviser / Planner
Works for: you
Helps you understand what you want to achieve and how your finances fit together. Plans, advises on tax, coordinates your whole financial life, and stays alongside you through change.
£1,500–£4,000 one-off planning + £2,000–£10,000+ p.a. ongoing
Xentum — this is us
Role 2
Custodian / Platform
Works for: you
Holds your investments securely and handles day-to-day administration — account setup, trades, statements, tax documents, and keeping your assets safe.
~0.15–0.40% p.a. (often capped at a maximum £ amount)
e.g. AJ Bell, Transact, Quilter
Role 3
Investment Manager
Works for: adviser and you
Decides how your money is invested — the asset mix, how it evolves over time, and how performance is monitored against your strategy and risk level.
~0.25–1.0% p.a. — included in Xentum's annual fee. No extra charge.
Xentum — also us, at no extra cost
Role 4
Fund Manager
Works for: all fund investors
Manages the investments inside a fund — deciding what's bought and sold. Their cost is built into the fund price, not billed separately to you.
~0.05–0.75% p.a. (built into the fund price)
e.g. Dimensional, Vanguard, Albion

Before You Start

A quick note before we begin.

I'm not here to win awards for my writing.

This e-book wasn't written to sound clever, academic, or impressive. It exists to get ideas out of my head and onto the page as clearly and honestly as possible.

The first version of this wasn't a book at all — it came from around 18 months of voice notes after a shower or on a long walk, hastily scribbled iPhone notes whilst holding my newborn baby, and insights from conversations Dominic and I have had sitting across the table from business owners over a combined 45+ years.

Talking about risk, timing, and the decisions people put off because they're uncomfortable to name.

AI helped to create this book.

But AI didn't create the thinking in this book. It didn't invent the ideas or experience the conversations. It simply organised what was already there and turned something messy into something readable.

The thinking in this book comes from years of doing this work properly — from real conversations, real decisions, and the experience of a team that has spent decades helping people make sense of money at moments that actually matter.

I'm trying to explain things the way they're actually experienced when you're the one carrying the responsibility.

If parts of this make you uncomfortable, that's probably a sign they're worth paying attention to.

That's the point. Let's begin.

Introduction

Why This Book Exists

If you're reading this, you probably don't think of yourself as reckless.

You've built something real. You've carried risk for years. You've navigated uncertainty that would overwhelm most people.

You know your market. You understand your customers. You've lived through cycles, shocks, and near-misses.

You don't need a lecture on risk tolerance.

And yet, for many founders at this stage, there's a quieter pressure running in the background:

"I need to get this decision right. Because if I get it wrong, I don't get another go."

This book exists because most business owners are running a form of risk that doesn't behave like the risks they're used to managing.

Not market risk. Not team risk. Not tax risk.

But concentrated risk over time, compounded by identity, responsibility, and life stage.

Most founders assume the riskiest moment is the sale itself.

In reality, a significant amount of risk sits before the sale — quietly accumulating while nothing appears broken.

The business feels stable. Cash flows. Customers stay. The team shows up. So the internal alarm never sounds.

That's the problem.

This book is not about selling your business.

It's about understanding the risk you're already running — and why intelligent, experienced people systematically misprice it.

If you've ever caught yourself thinking:

  • "One more year won't make much difference"
  • "We'll look at it properly when things calm down"
  • "I've handled worse than this"
  • "It's not risky — I control it"

Then this book is for you. Not because you're wrong. But because the way the human brain deals with uncertainty breaks down precisely in situations like yours.

Chapter 1

The Quiet Lie About Risk

Most founders carry the same unspoken belief:

Risk is what happens in markets. My business is stable because I control it.

This belief feels sensible. Markets are noisy. Headlines move prices. Assets are priced daily. Your business isn't.

There's no ticker flashing red. No daily price reminding you something could go wrong. No visible volatility.

So your nervous system quietly categorises it as safer. That's the first distortion.

Risk is not defined by how loud something is.

Risk is defined by what can permanently damage you.

A diversified portfolio can fall sharply and recover. A business concentrated in one owner, one geography, one management team, one life stage often cannot.

But because SME risk isn't priced daily, it hides. Losses are absorbed privately. Stress is normalised. Exposure feels familiar.

And familiarity is the most effective camouflage risk has.

Why Inaction Feels Sensible

The human brain did not evolve to optimise probabilistic outcomes over long time horizons. It evolved to conserve energy and avoid immediate regret.

When something is familiar and functioning, the brain stops actively reassessing it. Like driving a route you've taken hundreds of times, decisions begin to run on a stored loop.

Business continuation works the same way. As long as the business is familiar, functioning, producing income, and demanding known behaviours — the brain treats staying put as the lowest-effort option.

Action feels dangerous because it creates a clear before-and-after, introduces responsibility, and makes regret imaginable.

Inaction feels safe because nothing visibly changes, responsibility feels deferred, and outcomes remain hypothetical.

Neurologically, doing nothing is often classified as the lowest-risk choice, even when it isn't.

Why Control Feels Like Protection (But Isn't)

Founders confuse control with safety. You know your market. You understand your customers. You can influence outcomes. You've earned the right to back yourself.

But control doesn't eliminate risk — it concentrates it.

The more competent you are, the longer you're willing to carry exposure without questioning it. Experience quietly works against you here.

Hidden Volatility Is More Dangerous Than Visible Volatility

Visible volatility forces decisions. Markets fall. Prices move. Risk becomes undeniable.

Hidden volatility does the opposite. In a business, volatility shows up as longer hours, delayed investment, quiet stress, postponed personal plans, and subtle trade-offs no one else sees.

Volatility hasn't disappeared. It has been internalised by you.

This is why founders can be uneasy about market swings, yet calm about a single asset underwriting income, identity, lifestyle, family security, and future options. One is loud. The other is quiet. And the brain mistakes quiet for safe.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"What risk am I already running by not deciding?"

Chapter 2

Why Smart Founders Systematically Misprice Risk

If mispricing risk were a sign of incompetence, this book wouldn't exist.

The founders who struggle most with timing are rarely naïve, careless, or inexperienced. They are usually the opposite: disciplined, resilient, and used to carrying uncertainty better than most people around them.

Which is exactly why this problem hides for so long. The issue isn't that founders don't understand risk. It's that success rewires how risk feels.

Survival Teaches the Wrong Lesson

Every founder carries a private record of survival. The tough year that didn't break the business. The customer concentration that "worked out in the end." The cash crunch that resolved itself.

Each time this happens, the brain updates its internal model: "That was dangerous — and I handled it."

Over time, the lesson quietly shifts from "That was risky" to "This is manageable." This is not arrogance. It's conditioning.

As Kahneman and Tversky showed, the human brain learns primarily from outcomes, not probabilities. When things work out, we credit judgement. When they don't, we blame bad luck. That's outcome bias.

Good Decisions, Bad Outcomes — and the Reverse

Founders are trained to evaluate decisions by results. If it worked, it was a good decision. If it didn't, it was a bad one.

That logic works in operational environments where feedback is fast, errors are reversible, and decisions are repeatable. Exits are not like that. Exits are probabilistic, irreversible, path-dependent, and heavily influenced by external forces.

In these environments, a good decision can lead to a bad outcome — and a bad decision can be rescued by luck.

As Annie Duke puts it, the question is not "Did it work?" but "Was this the right decision given what I could reasonably know at the time?"

Why Drift Feels Safe — Until It Isn't

Drift is the most dangerous form of risk accumulation because it has no trigger point.

Think of a slow current in a river. At first, it feels negligible. You're still moving forward. Nothing feels urgent. But over time, you're carried further from the bank than you realise.

This is how founders drift into mispriced exits. Not through bad decisions — but through the absence of deliberate ones.

Time Is the Amplifier

Concentration is not static. It compounds with time. Every additional year of success increases dependency on a single asset, exposure to unforecastable events, and the cost of a bad outcome.

Long success does not reduce risk. It often masks it. And because nothing breaks, the brain sees no reason to reassess.

That is why confidence at this stage is not always a signal of safety. It is often a signal of exposure.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"Your confidence may be evidence of familiarity — not protection."

Chapter 3

Risk Is Not Volatility

Most conversations about risk start in the wrong place. They focus on movement — prices, markets, swings, headlines. Volatility feels like danger because it is visible. But volatility is not risk.

Volatility is movement. Risk is the chance of permanent damage.

Temporary Loss vs Permanent Loss

A diversified portfolio can fall sharply and recover. A concentrated business often cannot. The difference is not intelligence or effort. It's structure.

Temporary loss fluctuates, is uncomfortable, and can be waited out. Permanent loss removes options, changes trajectories, and cannot be undone.

Howard Marks has written for decades that risk is not about how much prices move — it's about what happens if you're wrong. Founders instinctively understand this in operations. A bad month is noise. Losing a key client, partner, or capability is structural. Yet many fail to apply the same logic to their own balance sheet.

Why Quiet Assets Feel Safer

Your business doesn't have a daily price. That absence creates a powerful illusion: no price movement means no visible loss, and no visible loss means no perceived risk.

But risk does not disappear when it isn't visible. It simply stops being measured.

If your business were priced daily, many owners would be shocked by how volatile their "stable" asset really is. But because the volatility is internalised, it never forces reassessment.

Concentration Is the Real Variable

Risk is magnified by concentration. Not just financial concentration — but life concentration. When one asset underwrites income, identity, lifestyle, family security, and future options simultaneously — the consequences of failure are asymmetric.

This is why founders often feel uneasy without being able to explain why. It's not fear. It's subconscious recognition of uncapped downside.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"What happens to me if things don't go well — and how long am I prepared to keep carrying that exposure?"

Chapter 4

Where SME Risk Actually Sits on the Spectrum

Most founders think they have a good handle on risk. They know cash feels safer than equities. They know diversification reduces volatility. They know speculation sits at the sharp end.

But when it comes to their own business, those instincts quietly fail. Not because the business is safer — because the risk is harder to see.

A More Honest Spectrum

If you strip away familiarity and look at structure rather than feeling, the picture changes.

Cash & short-dated government debt
Low volatility. Low return. Low permanent loss risk.

Diversified public equities
High visible volatility. Historically low probability of permanent loss over time.

Concentrated public equities
Higher downside risk, but still liquid and repriced continuously.

Single-company SME ownership
No visible volatility. Extreme concentration. High dependency on individuals, timing, health, and local conditions.

Venture capital / speculative assets
Only after this do you reach the traditional "high risk" category.

Here's the uncomfortable truth: a single SME often carries venture-level downside without venture-level upside.

Capped Upside, Uncapped Personal Cost

The upside of your business is capped by market multiples, buyer appetite, deal structure, and timing.

The downside is not. Downside includes loss of income, extended earn-outs, forced tie-ins, health deterioration, family strain, and identity collapse.

You might gain another turn of EBITDA. But you could lose years of optionality. That is asymmetric downside — and it's the kind the brain consistently underweights.

Why This Matters More Later in Life

The same business is not equally risky at every age. At 35, concentration risk is buffered by time, energy, recovery capacity, and identity flexibility. At 55, it isn't.

Health matters more. Family reliance is higher. Career recovery time is shorter. Tolerance for prolonged uncertainty is lower.

The asset hasn't changed. Your capacity to absorb a bad outcome has.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"Where does this asset sit on the spectrum of permanent damage — and how much of my remaining options are riding on it?"

Chapter 5

Concentration Builds Wealth — Then Turns Against You

Concentration is not a mistake. It's how wealth is built. Every meaningful business is created through focus: one idea, one market, one leadership vision, one owner carrying risk. Diversification comes later.

The mistake is not concentration. The mistake is failing to reprice it as life changes.

The Concentration Lifecycle

Concentration follows a predictable arc.

Creation phase: Concentration is rewarded. Risk feels justified. Energy is abundant.

Expansion phase: Concentration is tolerated. Returns grow. Options appear to increase.

Maturity phase: Concentration fades into the background. Success masks exposure. Risk feels normal.

Exit-adjacent phase: Concentration turns punitive. Life-stage risk rises. Downside accelerates.

Most founders understand this intellectually. Very few recalibrate emotionally.

Why "Just One More Year" Is So Dangerous

At this stage, a familiar sentence appears: "One more year won't make much difference."

Sometimes it doesn't. But sometimes it's the year where momentum slows, energy drops, buyer appetite shifts, and valuation certainty weakens.

This is how founders drift from clean exits into deferred consideration, earn-outs, and multi-year tie-ins. Not because the business failed. But because timing collided with life-stage.

Optimisation vs Survivability

Founders are trained to optimise: margins, systems, scale. Optimisation assumes a stable risk environment. Late-stage concentration breaks that assumption.

This is where survivability becomes the correct objective. Not "How much more can this be worth?" but:

"How do I make sure one bad path doesn't undo everything?"

That shift is not pessimism. It's maturity.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"How much concentrated exposure am I willing to keep carrying at this stage of my life?"

Chapter 6

The Timing Illusion: Why Waiting Feels Prudent (Until It Isn't)

Most founders don't delay because they're indecisive. They delay because waiting feels responsible. Measured. Rational. Adult.

Nothing is on fire. The business is trading. Customers are still there. The team turns up. From the outside, there's no reason to rush. That's the timing illusion.

The Psychological Clock vs the Calendar Clock

Founders are trained to track one clock: the calendar. Deal timelines. Tax years. Forecasts. Valuation cycles.

But there's a second clock that usually starts first — the psychological clock. It starts when you imagine a clean break, picture not being responsible for payroll, feel relief at the idea of being "out of the game."

From that point on, something shifts. Tolerance drops. Patience thins. Energy leaks. You may still be effective. But internally, you've begun to detach.

The problem arises when the psychological clock runs far ahead of the calendar clock. That gap creates pressure.

Optionality Decay (Defined)

Optionality decay is the gradual erosion of real options while perceived options remain unchanged.

Perceived optionality says: "I could always sell next year."

Actual optionality depends on buyer appetite, sector sentiment, personal energy, health, deal structures, and life stage. Those don't decay evenly. They narrow quietly — then suddenly.

That's why founders often say: "If I'd known then what I know now, I'd have acted earlier." Not because the outcome was obvious. But because the option set was wider before it collapsed.

The Real Cost of Waiting

Waiting has a cost, even when value rises. That cost is paid in optionality, negotiating leverage, emotional energy, tolerance for uncertainty, and family patience.

Upside moves slowly. Downside accelerates. Because downside is probabilistic, the brain discounts it. That's how waiting feels prudent — right up until it isn't.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"Which options am I assuming will still be there — and what if they aren't?"

Chapter 7

"Enough" Is Not a Lifestyle Number

When founders ask, "What's enough?", advisers often answer the wrong question. They hear holidays, houses, cars, spending levels. But that's not what founders are really asking.

"When does this stop feeling dangerous?"

The Threat Threshold (Formalised)

Every founder has a point — often unspoken — where exposure drops below a level that triggers constant vigilance. This is the threat threshold.

Below the threat threshold: decisions feel lighter, sleep improves, patience returns, generosity becomes easier, anxiety recedes.

Above the threat threshold: everything feels provisional, success never quite touches the sides, goalposts keep moving, risk feels omnipresent even in good years.

Threat thresholds are not lifestyle numbers. They are risk sufficiency numbers. They answer: "In a bad version of the future, are we still okay?"

Lifestyle Numbers Drift. Threat Thresholds Don't.

Lifestyle numbers are elastic — they move with peers, context, aspiration, and identity. Threat thresholds are anchored — driven by responsibility, dependants, health, age, and irreversibility.

That's why one founder can feel calm on £3m, while another feels exposed on £15m. The difference isn't ambition. It's where their threat threshold sits.

The Reframe That Matters

Once this clicks, the question shifts. Not "How much more could this be worth?" but:

"What level of exposure allows me to stand down vigilance — without relying on luck?"

That is the beginning of confidence. Not bravado. Not optimism. Structural confidence.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"When does this stop feeling dangerous?"

Chapter 8

Risk Doesn't End When You Decide to Sell — It Moves

One of the most common misconceptions about exit planning is that selling solves the risk problem. It doesn't. It relocates it.

Before a sale, risk is concentrated, illiquid, and identity-loaded. After a sale, risk becomes visible, diversified, and discussable. Neither state is risk-free. But one is choosable.

The Visibility Shock

When a business sells, founders often experience something unexpected: the sudden visibility of risk they had been carrying quietly for years.

When the business was private, its risk was absorbed internally — through effort, attention, and personal exposure. Now those risks are priced. Named. Tracked daily.

This is disorienting. Not because markets are more volatile than the business was, but because the volatility is now visible. And visibility feels like danger, even when the underlying exposure is lower.

How Risk Enters the Family System

Post-exit risk is rarely individual. It enters the family system.

Partners who weren't involved in the business now have visible opinions about money decisions. Children become aware of wealth in new ways. Family dynamics that were stable under a shared "business owner" identity can shift when that identity dissolves.

The financial plan has to account for this. Not just asset allocation — but how decisions are made together, how values are communicated, and how wealth is held in a way that doesn't create more friction than it resolves.

Human Capital Was Always the Anchor

Throughout the business-owning years, the founder's human capital — judgement, energy, resilience, relationships — was the real anchor of the enterprise. The business value was, in many ways, a reflection of that.

After the exit, that human capital doesn't disappear. But its economic expression changes. The question becomes: what do you deploy it into next?

The founders who struggle most post-exit are often those who answer "nothing" — not because they're lazy, but because they haven't had space to imagine what comes next.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"What do I want to be responsible for next — and what am I choosing to set down?"

Chapter 9

How Good Decisions Are Made Under Uncertainty

The founders who exit well don't exit with certainty. They exit with a decision structure that allows them to live well with whatever happens.

That's a different objective than most assume.

Decision Quality vs Decision Outcome

Most founders evaluate exit decisions the same way they evaluate operational decisions: by what happened next.

But exit decisions are one-time, irreversible, and path-dependent. The outcome depends on forces far beyond the decision quality. Markets move. Buyers change. Circumstances shift.

A good decision made in imperfect conditions can still lead to a difficult outcome. A poorly structured decision can be rescued by luck.

Decision quality must be judged independently of outcome. That means asking not "did it work?" but "was this the right call given what I could reasonably know?"

What High-Quality Exit Decisions Optimise For

Survivability over optimisation
Protecting against the bad version of the future, not just chasing the good one.

Reversibility where possible
Preferring structures that preserve optionality over those that lock in an outcome.

Downside that's liveable
Not removing risk — redesigning where it sits, so the worst case is one you can absorb.

Decision criteria, not outcome criteria
Knowing in advance what a good process looks like, not just what a good result looks like.

Risk Is Unavoidable — Allocation Is a Choice

A common misconception is that selling the business is about removing risk. It isn't. It's about choosing where risk sits next.

Before: concentrated, illiquid, identity-loaded. After: diversified, visible, discussable. Neither state is risk-free. But one is choosable. That choice is the real work of an exit.

The Shift That Changes Everything

The moment founders stop asking "What is the right answer?" and start asking:

"What decision structure gives me the best chance of living well with whatever happens?"

The pressure changes. Confidence becomes structural — not emotional. That is the point of this book.

The question this chapter leaves you with

"What decision allows me and my family to live well — whatever happens next?"

Closing

What Cashing Out Actually Means

By now, one thing should be clear. This book was never really about selling your business. It was about understanding the risk you were already running — and deciding whether you want to keep carrying it.

Liquidity Is a Transaction. Closure Is a State.

Liquidity changes your personal balance sheet. Closure changes your nervous system.

You can be liquid and still feel on edge, unfinished, mentally entangled, unsure whether you did the right thing. And you can have less liquidity than expected and still feel settled, clear, able to stand down vigilance.

The difference is not price. It's whether the decision ended a chapter cleanly.

Closure happens when:

— the risk has been deliberately reallocated

— the downside is survivable

— the future no longer depends on one fragile asset

— responsibility has been consciously reshaped

That's when relief arrives. Not as euphoria. As quiet.

Identity Doesn't End — It Transitions

Many founders worry, quietly, about who they'll be without the business. Not what they'll do — but who they'll be.

Selling doesn't erase that identity. It releases it from being tied to one asset. What comes next isn't retreat. It's redeployment: judgement, perspective, pattern recognition, capital, time.

The Point of All This

If this book has done its job, it hasn't told you what to do. It's helped you see the risk you were already running, the cost of waiting without deciding, the difference between optimisation and survivability, and why timing is psychological as much as financial.

Most of all, it's reframed the real question. Not "What's the perfect outcome?" but:

"What decision allows me and my family to live well — whatever happens next?"

That's what it actually means to cash out with confidence.

Not certainty. But closure.

And once you have that, the next chapter stops feeling like an escape. It starts feeling like a choice.

The four things we stand for

Values aren't words. They're decisions.

Every firm in financial services claims to act in their clients' best interests. Very few are willing to show you, in specific structural terms, how they've organised themselves to do exactly that. These four values aren't aspirational — they're the commitments we've actually built the business around.

01
Transparency

We show our working

Our fees are published in full before any conversation takes place. Every conflict of interest we carry is named, explained, and accompanied by the specific action we take to manage it. 02
Authenticity

We are who we say we are

We don't have a marketing version of Xentum and a real version. The story on this website is the same story our clients experience. Our advisers are shareholders, not salespeople. Our founding story — the experience that made Dominic build this firm — is the same one that guides every decision we make. Authenticity means there's no gap between what we say and what we do.

03
Honesty

We say what needs saying

We tell prospective clients when we're not right for them. We recommend paying down mortgages when that serves people better than investing with us. We tell clients when their cover is excessive. Honesty sometimes costs us revenue — and we think that's exactly as it should be. A financial planner who only says what you want to hear is not a financial planner worth having.

04
Fun

Serious work, serious enjoyment

Financial planning matters enormously. It also doesn't have to feel like a dental appointment. We enjoy what we do, we enjoy the people we work with, and we believe that clients who genuinely like their advisers are more likely to be honest with them — and more likely to end up with a plan that actually works. Life is short. We choose to spend it well.

Why this matters

Society has a trust problem. Our industry reflects it.

Trust in institutions has been declining for decades. In financial services, that decline is earned. The most common fee model — charging a percentage of the money you manage — means that an adviser's income grows as your invested assets grow. On the surface, that looks like alignment. Look closer and the problem emerges: it creates subtle pressure to keep more of your money invested, even when paying off a mortgage or holding more cash might serve you better.

It means a client with £1.5m invested pays five times more than a client with £300,000 — for what is often the same service. The decisions made — or not made — shape entire lives: whether someone retires with enough, whether their family is protected, whether a business exit leaves them financially free or financially precarious. Most people have no framework for knowing what good advice looks like, what questions to ask, or when they're being failed.

We decided to fix that — starting with ourselves. Not with words, but with structure: how we charge, how we're owned, and what we publish.

The Xentum response

What we built instead

Xentum was designed from the beginning to address the structural problems in the industry. Not with words — with structure, with ownership arrangements, with transparent fees, with written commitments.

Advisers who own the business

At Xentum, our advisers are shareholders. Their long-term financial interest is tied to the firm's long-term reputation — not to the volume of products they place. An adviser who damages client trust today damages the value of their own shareholding tomorrow. That alignment is structural, not motivational.

What we don't do
Pay advisers bonuses for hitting sales targets
Reward advisers for the volume of products they place
Incentivise advisers to grow assets under management
Tie adviser income to short-term revenue targets
What we do instead
Pay all advisers a salary — no commission, no bonus
Give advisers a shareholding in the business
Measure success by client outcomes, not sales volumes
Cap client numbers per adviser — never more than they can properly serve

Fixed fees, not percentage of assets

When we modelled the full picture, what looked like an urgent exit turned into a considered partial one. They didn't rush. They made a decision they could stand behind. The Wheel gave them language for a conversation they hadn't been able to have.

Property business founders · Manchester
"

"I just want to turn left on the airplane three times a year." That was his retirement goal — a GP who'd spent 25 years running his own practice. Simple, specific, and completely his own. We built his plan backwards from that number. He didn't need to know about asset allocation first. He needed to know whether the practice sale would fund the life he'd been imagining.

GP & practice owner · South East
"

One of his three priorities was to take his kids on a three-week cultural adventure every single year — not someday, now, while they're still listening. He didn't want to just leave them a pile of money. He wanted to give them something he considered more valuable: experiences as a family. We structured his finances around that goal, and worked with Xentum Adventures to start planning the first trip.

Business owner · Client since 2024

The autopilot is expensive

Most business owners are running on autopilot when it comes to their personal finances. The business is the priority. Everything else gets dealt with later. But "later" has a cost — in missed tax planning, underinsured families, and a sale that happens without clarity on what enough actually means.

Grabbing life isn't about spending more or saving less. It's about clicking out of autopilot and making deliberate choices — about time, money, and what success actually looks like for you.

A question we ask in every first meeting:

"If we listed everything that was a priority in your life right now — and you scored 1–10 how satisfied you are with each — what would your total be? And what would it take to move every number up by just one point?"

The interactive version takes about 20 minutes. It's the same exercise we use in our first meeting with every new client — and it's free to try on your own.

Xentum · Transparency

Conflicts of interest.
Named and managed.

Most financial planning firms have a page on their website that says, in one form or another, "we act in your best interest at all times." We've always thought that's not enough. We decided to do something harder: name every conflict of interest we carry, explain why it exists, and show the specific actions we take to manage it.

This is not a regulatory box-tick. It's a direct consequence of the reason Xentum exists.

Commission

Life cover and income protection:
we receive commission — here's why

Why we accept commission on protection

We believe everyone who needs protection should have it. A fixed advice fee — even a modest one — can make a straightforward life insurance policy feel prohibitively expensive. Commission allows us to arrange appropriate protection for every client, regardless of premium size, without creating a financial barrier to something fundamentally important.

  • We research the whole market
    Our recommendation is based on the best policy for your circumstances — not the highest commission rate.
  • We disclose commission amounts in writing
    Every protection recommendation comes with a written disclosure of the commission we'll receive — the amount, from whom, and when. You'll see this before the policy is placed.
  • No advisers receive commission personally
    Commission goes to the firm, not to individual advisers as a bonus. Our advisers are salaried. There is no internal incentive to recommend more or more expensive cover.
  • You can always switch to a fee arrangement
    If you'd prefer us to work on a fee basis and rebate any commission received, we'll do that. Just ask.
Other known conflicts

How we manage the conflicts we can't eliminate

Some conflicts are structural — built into the way advice businesses operate. We can't eliminate them, but we can name them and show what we do about them.

Known conflicts — and how we manage them
Our ongoing fees are linked to assets under advice

This creates a subtle incentive to keep assets invested with us rather than advising a client to pay down a mortgage. How we manage it: We've moved deliberately towards fixed and tiered fees. We regularly model scenarios that include reducing investments — and recommend them when they're right.

We have preferred investment partners

We work with Albion Strategic Consulting and typically recommend AJ Bell. These aren't random choices — but they create relationships that could, in theory, bias our thinking. How we manage it: We review our recommendations regularly against the whole market. We're regulated to justify every recommendation.

We benefit when clients stay with us long-term

Client retention is good for our business — which could create pressure to tell clients what they want to hear. How we manage it: We actively train against this. We offer a money-back guarantee because we'd rather lose a fee than keep a client who isn't benefiting from our service.

We're not neutral on property vs. investment

Our expertise and revenue centre on financial planning and investment advice. Clients with significant property wealth may not get fully balanced guidance from us on that element. How we manage it: We're transparent about this limitation and refer clients to specialists when needed.

Any questions?

If something here raises a question, ask us directly. We mean it.

Xentum · Careers

We hire on values
and attitude.

Technical skills can be taught. The way someone thinks about clients, about honesty, about what it means to do this work properly — that's much harder to change. We hire for the latter first.

How we hire

Values first.
Qualifications second.

Every member of the Xentum team — from our Chartered planners to our client support team — was hired because of how they think about people and their work, not just what they know. Qualifications matter and we support everyone to achieve them. But they're the threshold, not the deciding factor.

Our values aren't something we put on the wall. They're what we look for at interview, what we assess in probation, and what we build the team's culture around. We're a small firm. One person who doesn't share the values creates noise that the whole team feels.

01
Transparency

We look for people who are honest about what they don't know and clear about what they do. No performance. No spin.

02
Authenticity

We want people who are the same in every room — with clients, with colleagues, and when nobody's watching.

03
Honesty

We look for people who say what needs saying — even when it's uncomfortable. Especially when it's uncomfortable.

04
Fun

We take the work seriously. We don't take ourselves too seriously. Life is too short not to enjoy what you do.

What we look for

The things we can't train into someone

When we interview, we're looking for evidence of certain things that we've found are either present in someone or not. Experience level matters far less than you'd expect.

  • Genuine curiosity about people
    Financial planning is a relationship business. We look for people who are actually interested in the humans sitting across the table — not just the numbers in their pension.
  • Comfort with difficult conversations
    We tell clients things they sometimes don't want to hear. We look for people who don't shy away from that — who understand that honesty is a form of care.
  • Pride in the quality of their work
    We're a small team. Every piece of work is visible. We look for people who care about getting things right, not just getting them done.
  • Long-term thinking
    Most of our client relationships span decades. We want people who see that the same way we do — as a responsibility and a privilege, not just a job.
What we don't hire for

We're not a good fit for everyone

We're deliberately honest about this. Some people thrive in environments with large sales targets, commission-driven pay, and a fast churn of clients. That's not us — and we'd rather say so upfront.

Sales targets or volume metrics as the primary measure of success

Article · FIRE & Wealth

When Success Becomes
the Problem

You built wealth the FIRE way — index funds, low fees, long horizons. Now there's a lot more of it. Here's what changes, what doesn't, and what you need to think about next.

15 min read FIRE Investing Relevant to all clients

There's a peculiar moment that many FIRE-minded investors reach — usually after a business exit, an inheritance, or a run of exceptional investment growth — when the philosophy that served them brilliantly starts to feel insufficient. The strategy was perfect when the pot was £200,000. Now it's £5 million, or £10 million, or more. While the core principles haven't changed, the execution has become genuinely complex.

This is not a comfortable thing to admit if you've spent years reading Bogle, following the Boglehead forums, and rightly concluding that most financial advisers aren't worth what they charge. The FIRE movement is built on a liberating insight: passive index investing, low costs, and patience beat almost everything else. That insight remains true. What changes is the landscape around it.

When assets grow large enough, the game shifts. Tax optimisation stops being a marginal concern and becomes a six-figure decision. Estate planning stops being something you'll deal with eventually and starts carrying real urgency. And the question "where do I put this?" stops having a simple, obvious answer.

The FIRE Foundation Still Holds

Before diving into what changes, it's worth restating what doesn't. The evidence base for passive investing is, if anything, stronger now than when Jack Bogle launched Vanguard's first index fund in 1976. The academic research underpinning this — including Eugene Fama and Kenneth French's factor models — shows that low-cost, diversified, long-term investing outperforms active stock picking for the vast majority of investors over the vast majority of time periods.

You don't abandon this because you have more money. The core portfolio — broad global equities, low-cost funds, appropriate bond allocation — remains the engine. What you're building at this stage is a more sophisticated vehicle around it.

"With a smaller portfolio, the main risk is under-saving or panic-selling. With a larger one, the risks become more varied: tax drag compounding over decades, inheritance tax eroding what you pass on, and the psychological challenge of managing assets that feel almost abstract in their scale."

The Tax Picture Gets Much More Complicated

Capital Gains Tax

If you've received a significant lump sum from a business sale, the CGT calculation becomes critical — and in some situations deeply ambiguous. The treatment of shares received as part of a deal, earn-outs, and proceeds held briefly in escrow can all affect your liability in ways that aren't always obvious. This is not territory for a generalist accountant who does your annual self-assessment alongside fifty others. You need a specialist.

Equally important: don't rush to invest funds that will be needed in the short term. If you have a known tax liability due in January, or a property purchase on the horizon within the next year or two, that money should not be in equities. Short-dated UK government bonds (gilts) have become an increasingly attractive holding for known near-term obligations — they're free of capital gains tax, meaning your return on a discounted gilt bought to maturity is entirely a capital gain, and therefore tax-free.

The Ongoing Wrapper Question

Within an ISA or SIPP, growth and income are sheltered. Within a General Investment Account (GIA), you're paying income tax on dividends and CGT on gains. One practical consequence: for GIA holdings, accumulating funds (which reinvest dividends internally) can be more efficient than distributing ones, since you're not forced to realise income each year. But when drawing down, selling units as needed is typically both cleaner and more tax-efficient than switching to income share classes.

Holding Company Structures

You may encounter suggestions to invest through a holding or family investment company (FIC). The appeal is real: dividends between companies are largely tax-free. But the complexity is also real — legal costs, accounting costs, and inflexibility. The honest advice from experienced planners is often simply: don't do it yet. Retain your flexibility. Simplicity is almost always the right starting point, and complexity should only be introduced when the benefit clearly outweighs the cost.

Inheritance Tax: The Problem You Didn't Expect

Many FIRE investors haven't thought much about inheritance tax (IHT) because, until recently, their estate simply wasn't large enough. Once you cross certain thresholds, it becomes very relevant very quickly.

In the UK, IHT is charged at 40% on the value of your estate above the nil-rate bands. The main nil-rate band is £325,000. There is a residence nil-rate band of up to £175,000, but this tapers to zero for estates above £2 million. For a person with an estate of £8 million, the effective IHT liability on death could exceed £3 million.

40%
IHT rate above the nil-rate threshold
£325k
Main nil-rate band per person
7 yrs
For outright gifts to leave the estate

The key insight is that none of the mitigation strategies require urgency. If you're in your 30s or 40s, in good health, the sensible move is often simply to note the liability, understand the options, and maintain flexibility. Making an irrevocable decision to deal with an IHT problem twenty years early often means sacrificing more in flexibility and cost than you gain in tax saving.

What Vanguard's Own Research Says About Advisers

It's worth noting that the most rigorous research on the value of financial advice comes not from the adviser industry, but from Vanguard itself — whose index funds underpin the FIRE philosophy. Their Adviser's Alpha framework attempts to quantify exactly what a good adviser adds.

"An adviser following best practices can add up to 3% in net returns annually. Almost none of that value comes from investment selection or market timing — it comes from behavioural coaching, tax-efficient wrapper use, and withdrawal sequencing."

The single largest component is behavioural coaching, which Vanguard estimates can add up to 200 basis points. The reason is simple: the most costly mistakes investors make are not picking the wrong fund, but reacting emotionally to market events. Selling during the Covid crash of March 2020 and re-entering once markets had recovered cost investors around 25 percentage points of return compared with those who stayed the course.

Vanguard also puts significant value — up to 112 basis points — on tax-efficient withdrawal sequencing alone: which accounts to draw from, and in what order, during the accumulation-to-drawdown transition. At significant wealth levels, getting this wrong is an expensive and entirely avoidable mistake.

What Financial Independence Actually Means

There is a persistent misunderstanding about what the FI in FIRE represents. Financial independence is not, at its core, about stopping work. It's about removing financial compulsion from the decision to work. When work is optional, your relationship to it transforms. You no longer tolerate bad clients or businesses you've outgrown because you have to. You take on things that interest you because you want to.

For someone who has built and sold a business, this reframe is worth sitting with. The exit doesn't mean the end of ambition or purpose. It means those things are now decoupled from financial survival. The next project, if it happens, happens because it's genuinely compelling — not because the mortgage requires it.

"The goal was never really to stop. It was to have enough that stopping became a genuine choice rather than an impossible dream."

A person in their late thirties or early forties who has achieved financial independence might have fifty years of adult life ahead. A plan that treats those fifty years as a long holiday is not a serious plan. What most people in this position actually want — whether they articulate it this way or not — is to remain engaged, keep building things, stay useful, while having the security of knowing none of it is financially desperate.

The Principles That Got You Here Still Apply

FIRE is not a strategy for small portfolios. It's a philosophy: own the market, minimise costs, think long term, and don't try to be clever when simple works. Those principles scale.

What changes at higher levels of wealth is the context around the portfolio. Tax matters more. Estate planning matters more. The right professional relationships — a good accountant, a fixed-fee financial planner who believes in evidence-based investing, possibly a specialist tax adviser — matter more than they once did. Not because you can no longer think for yourself, but because the decisions are now complex enough that even a well-informed person benefits from expert input.

The core is still a diversified global equity portfolio in low-cost index funds, held for decades. The wrapper, the tax structure, the estate plan, the professional relationships — those are the things that change when the numbers get bigger. Getting those right is the new challenge. And unlike picking stocks, it's a challenge with a reasonably clear and manageable answer.

Cash Out With Confidence

The financial planning guide for business owners actively preparing to exit — and determined to get it right. Written by Ed Stubbs, Chartered Financial Planner, Xentum.

Xentum Financial Planning

Cash Out With Confidence

A guide for business owners actively preparing to exit

2025 / 26 Edition

Most exit guides are written for accountants, not for founders. They talk about deal structures and EBITDA multiples and miss the question most business owners actually lie awake thinking about.

Which is: Will this be enough? And what comes next?

This guide is written for founders who are 12–24 months from a sale and want to approach the biggest financial transaction of their lives with clarity, not anxiety. It will not tell you what your business is worth — that is your accountant's job. What it will do is help you understand, probably for the first time, what the sale needs to do for you and your life.

Contents
1The exit nobody fully prepares for
2Getting the timing right
3Know your number — not somebody else's
4The tax landscape in 2025/26
5From offence to defence
6Purpose after the exit
7Protecting your family
8Building your exit team
Chapter 1

The exit nobody fully prepares for

One of the strangest feelings in the world — and one that very few people ever experience — is logging into your bank account and seeing £15,000,000 sitting there. It sounds like a problem most people would love to have. And in many ways, it is. But it comes with its own particular disorientation, one that nobody warns you about.

"You get a few weeks of euphoria. A nice holiday. And then the real questions start coming. I had no idea what to do with the money, whether I'd got enough, or what I was supposed to do with myself."A founder we spoke to, six weeks after completion

The best advice we have ever heard from a founder who sold an eight-figure business? "Do nothing." Sit with it. Decompress. Resist the urge to immediately reinvest, restructure, or reinvent yourself. Give yourself permission to pause. Clarity on the next chapter takes time — but it is worth waiting for.

That said, the work that prevents this disorientation does not start after the sale. It starts now. Long before the deal is on the table. This guide is about that work.

Chapter 2

Are you ready? Getting the timing right

The most common timing mistake business owners make is not leaving it too late. It is convincing themselves that there will be a better moment — a cleaner moment — just around the corner. And so they keep going.

That phrase — removing the risk — is important. Business owners are trained to think about risk as something attached to inaction. But concentrated risk is equally, if not more, dangerous. If more than 75% of your net worth sits in a single private business — one that is not priced daily, one that you cannot sell with a click — you are taking on a level of risk that most people would find difficult to justify rationally.

Signals that the time may be right:

  • You are no longer fighting fires — the business runs without you at the centre of everything
  • There is genuine market demand — you have received unsolicited approaches from buyers
  • Your personal health, energy or priorities have shifted
  • You have not had a holiday in years where you truly switched off
  • The thought of "going again" for another three to five years fills you with exhaustion, not excitement
  • The external environment is changing faster than it used to
  • You have a clear sense that the business has reached a natural inflection point

None of these are definitive. But if three or more resonate with you, the timing conversation is worth having — not with a buyer, but with someone who can help you understand what an exit would actually mean for your life.

The average UK business sale takes around eight months from instruction to completion. Add in the preparation phase and three years is a reasonable horizon for a genuinely well-executed exit. Around three-quarters of business sales that reach Heads of Terms subsequently fall through before completion. The earlier you start preparing, the more control you retain over the outcome.

Chapter 3

Know your number — not somebody else's

Here is something we hear regularly: a business owner has a figure in their head. It is usually a round number. £1m, £3m, £5m, £10m. Or they have based it on what somebody at their golf club sold for. The problem? That number has almost nothing to do with them. It is somebody else's context applied to their life.

The question we help owners answer is not: What will the business sell for? It is: What does the sale need to achieve for your life? Those are very different questions — and answering the second one changes everything about how you approach the first.

Only around one in ten business owners truly knows what is enough for them. The rest guess. And they mostly guess wrong — either overestimating (and holding out for a figure that costs them years), or underestimating (and walking away not knowing if they made a mistake).

The Xentum Enough Number Formula
 Your values, life priorities and the true cost of your desired lifestyle
+An accurate picture of your current assets, income and liabilities
+Evidence-based modelling assumptions (run to age 100)
+The right stress tests: "What if we spend £400k a year? What if it's £700k?"
=Clarity on the sale value that can confidently fund the life you and your family want

We run models to age 100. We stress-test them against different spending levels, market conditions, and life events. We ask: when does the money actually run out? That is the answer that tells you what you really need.

Chapter 4

The tax landscape in 2025/26

Tax planning in the context of a business exit is not a last-minute exercise. The October 2024 Budget introduced the most significant changes to business exit taxation in years, and understanding them is now an urgent priority for anyone planning to sell.

Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) — the window is closing:

PeriodBADR Rate (gains up to £1m)Standard CGT Rate
Up to April 202510%24%
2025/26 tax year14%24%
From April 2026 onwards18%24%

If you are a business owner with a SIPP or SSAS, a sale event creates a significant opportunity to maximise pension funding — often the most tax-efficient route available. You can currently contribute up to £60,000 per year through the annual allowance, with unused allowance carried forward from the previous three years.

Business Property Relief (BPR) currently allows shares in qualifying trading companies to pass free of IHT on death. Post-sale, once those shares become cash, that relief disappears. Planning ahead — through trusts, structured gifting strategies, and appropriate life cover — can protect family wealth significantly.

Many of the most effective tax planning strategies need to be implemented well before formal sale negotiations begin. By the time a buyer is in the room, your options reduce significantly.
Chapter 5

From offence to defence

For twenty or thirty years, concentration has been your strategy. You backed yourself. You took risk where others would not. That mindset built your wealth. But it is not the mindset that protects it.

We think about this like a football match. For years you have been playing on the attack. But at some point in the game, you are protecting a lead. The job is no longer to score more goals. It is to make sure you do not lose the ones you have.

When we model post-sale portfolios properly, the answer is often simpler than founders expect. You might only need a 3–4% long-term return to fund everything you want for the rest of your life. That changes the risk you need to take on completely.

"Three years ago my mindset was: push it, chase 10–15% returns through complex structures, keep winning. Now? Simplicity and defence over attack. Do we actually need that level of risk? What return do we really need?"A founder, three years after selling an eight-figure business
Chapter 6

The part nobody talks about: purpose after the exit

Every exit planning conversation eventually gets to the money. Not enough of them get to this part.

We have seen too many founders go from one hundred percent to nothing overnight. And it does not work. Not for most of them. The most resonant line we have encountered — from a financial planner who works with lottery winners — is this: sudden wealth is a test of your existing values. It gives you the opportunity to align yourself, and the time and energy you expend, to what genuinely matters to you.

At our first meeting with every founder, we spend time on the Grab Life Wheel — a life exercise, not a financial one. We ask you to identify the areas of life that genuinely matter, rank them, score your current happiness in each, and describe what a nine or ten out of ten looks like. For couples, the results are almost always different — and the conversation that follows is often one of the most valuable they have had in years.

Our advice to every founder approaching an exit: do the values work before you talk to buyers. Understand what the next thirty years looks like for you and your family. Build the financial model around that picture. Then you walk into buyer conversations knowing exactly what you need from the deal — and what good looks like on the other side.

Chapter 7

Protecting your family: the estate and the people who matter

You will leave your business in one of four ways. You will sell it. You will walk away from it. You will get pushed out. Or you will leave in a box. Most founders have a plan for the first. Very few have a plan for the other three.

Outdated Wills are one of the most common issues we encounter. Post-sale, when your business equity converts to cash, Inheritance Tax planning becomes particularly important — Business Property Relief disappears the moment those shares become cash. Planning needs to happen before that conversion, not after.

From April 2027, unused pension funds and death benefits are expected to be brought within the scope of Inheritance Tax for the first time. If your pension pot forms a significant part of your post-exit wealth, this changes the calculus of estate planning considerably — and it is worth reviewing now.

Chapter 8

Building your exit team — and how to keep them coordinated

One of the biggest structural risks in the exit process: the founder stuck in the middle, acting as translator between their corporate finance adviser, their tax specialist, their lawyers, and their financial planner — each doing excellent work in their own lane, but none of them seeing the full picture.

What we do at Xentum is not replace any of these specialists. It is to act as the quarterback — making sure your tax, legal, and investment advice all serve one joined-up plan. Because the context we have — built over hours of conversation about what matters to you and your family — is context the rest of the deal team cannot always see.

We know whether a deal structured with deferred consideration actually works for your lifestyle needs. We know whether taking shares rather than cash in an acquirer creates a risk profile you are comfortable with. We know what the earn-out period means for your family, your health, and your sense of purpose.

Introduction

The Movement of Clarity

Money shapes every major decision a family makes — yet most people have no clear framework for choosing a financial adviser, understanding fees, or knowing what 'good' advice even looks like.

This guide exists because real families have been hurt by a lack of education and, at times, poor guidance. Xentum's founder, Dominic Baldwin, and his family experienced bad advice first-hand. His father, from a farming background in Cumbria, inherited a significant sum at a young age. When he died, Dominic uncovered a long trail of poor decisions downstream of thinly veiled sales tactics wrapped up as 'professional guidance'.

"He didn't need a sales pitch and somebody only in the room to benefit themselves. He needed an honest, authentic, and genuine guide."

This guide is written to ensure you never feel in the dark about how financial decisions are made or who you're trusting with your family's future. We provide these resources to support you on that journey — and our goal is simply to help you make the best possible decision, even if that ultimately leads you to work with someone else.

To emphasise our commitment to transparency, the final edit of this guide went through the following AI prompt: "Is there any bias from the perspective of Xentum in writing this guide? If so, highlight which sections show bias and suggest unbiased alternatives." We addressed every flag.

What this guide covers

How the advice industry works · How advisers get paid · Where value is created (and where it isn't) · What a proper financial plan should include · How to avoid the most common and costly mistakes

Chapter 1

What does financial advice really cost?

Buying financial advice is a bit like creating and looking after a garden. You start with a design — deciding what you want to grow and how the space should work. Then everything needs to be planted and set up properly. After that, the garden needs regular care: watering, pruning, adjusting as the seasons change. That's why financial advice is usually priced as a long-term relationship, not a one-off transaction.

The three core components

1
The Financial Plan
Building the blueprint
Gathering financial information, understanding goals, building projections, producing a clear written plan. Typical cost: £2,500–£5,000 for most situations; up to £7,000+ for complex cases.
2
Implementation
Putting the plan into action
Opening accounts, moving money, recommending and setting up investments. Typical cost: 0.25%–1.0% per year of assets managed.
3
Ongoing Advice
Keeping the plan relevant
Regular reviews, monitoring, adjusting as life changes, behavioural coaching. Typical cost: £2,000–£15,000+ per year as a fixed fee, or 0.5%–1.0% of assets.

The four roles behind the scenes

Most confusion in financial advice comes down to one issue — people don't know who does what and what they're paying for. Before you decide how to work with a financial adviser, it's essential to understand the different roles involved in managing your money.

1
Financial Adviser / Planner
Helps you understand goals, builds your financial plan, coordinates everything, supports you over time. Acts as your main point of guidance.
£1,500–£4,000 one-off + £2,000–£10,000+/yr or ~0.5–1.0% p.a.
2
Custodian / Platform
Holds your investments securely, handles administration, carries out trades, provides statements and tax documents. Keeps your assets safe.
~0.15%–0.40% p.a. (often capped)
3
Investment Manager
Looks after how your money is invested within your accounts — decides asset allocation, makes changes over time, monitors performance.
~0.25%–1.0% p.a. depending on complexity
4
Fund Manager
Decides how investments inside a fund are managed. Their choices affect fund performance, but they don't look at your wider situation.
~0.05%–0.75% p.a. (built into fund price)
The Xentum model (example)

Xentum provides financial advice · AJ Bell acts as platform and custodian · Albion manages the portfolio · Dimensional & Vanguard manage the underlying funds. Each has a distinct role, a separate cost, and a different impact on your outcomes.

How fee structures shape adviser behaviour

The most common fee model in UK financial advice is a percentage of assets under management (AUM). Around 70% of advisers use this model. It means the adviser's income rises as your invested assets grow — and falls if they shrink.

On the surface, this looks like aligned incentives. But it creates some less obvious dynamics: a subtle bias toward keeping more of your money invested, even when paying down a mortgage or holding cash might serve you better. It also means a client with £1.5m invested pays five times more than a client with £300,000 — for what is often the same service.

Ask any prospective adviser: "What does my fee actually pay for?" · "Would my fee change if my portfolio value rose or fell?" · "Is there a cap or tiered structure?" Understanding this puts you in a much stronger position to evaluate fair value.

Chapter 2

What level of advice do you actually need?

Not everyone needs the same level of financial advice. The right scope depends less on how much money you have, and more on how complex your situation is and how much support you want.

0
Level 0
Self-Directed (DIY / Robo)
You manage investments yourself via platforms like Hargreaves Lansdown or robo-advisers like Nutmeg. Efficient and low-cost, but no personalised advice, no behavioural coaching, no professional helping you make decisions about your whole financial life.
1
Level 1
Transactional / Single-Issue Advice
Guidance on one specific decision — transferring a pension, choosing an ISA fund. No long-term planning, no modelling, no ongoing partnership. Best for: very simple financial needs or one-off clarity.
2
Level 2
Financial Advice
Retirement planning, investment strategy, basic tax planning, protection, annual review. Usually investment-led — the conversation often starts with "How should your money be invested?" rather than "What kind of life are you trying to build?"
3
Level 3
Full Financial Planning (Life-Centred)
Starts with your life, not your investments. Detailed cashflow modelling to age 100+, tax strategy, estate planning, business-owner planning, behavioural coaching, coordination with accountants and solicitors. Best for: major transitions, business owners, families with complex finances.
A useful signal on scope

Advisers with 100+ client reviews on VouchedFor are likely operating at Level 2. Genuine Level 3 financial planners work with 50–60 clients maximum per adviser — the depth of service required means they can't serve more than that properly.

Chapter 3

Which type of financial advice is right for you?

Before choosing the type of advice you need, you need to understand something most consumers never hear: there is no single adviser type who sits neutrally above both property and investment decisions. Property specialists recommend property. Financial advisers recommend portfolios, pensions, and tax wrappers. Understanding this bias matters before you choose.

The four types of advice

TypeLevel 1Level 2Level 3Notes
DIY / Self-Directed✗ No✗ No✗ NoTools to invest, not to plan
Robo-Advice⚠ Partial✗ No✗ NoAutomates DIY; limited scope
Restricted Advice✓ Yes✓ Yes⚠ SometimesProduct limits may affect complex needs
Independent (IFA)✓ Yes✓ Yes⚠ SometimesNot all IFAs offer deep life-centred planning
The key insight

Full financial planning is a scope, not a firm type. It can be delivered by restricted or independent firms. What matters most is the planning process — not whether the adviser is independent or restricted. DIY and robo cannot offer it.

Beware the behaviour gap (DIY & Robo)

Morningstar's long-term research shows that the gap between fund returns and actual investor returns typically ranges from 1%–2% per year — caused by buying after markets rise and selling when they fall. Over 20 years, even a 1.5% annual gap can reduce total wealth by more than 30%. Markets usually work. Staying invested is the hard part.

Chapter 4

Is your financial setup ready for advice?

Your current financial setup influences both the type of advice you need and how effectively that advice can be delivered. Some situations are straightforward and ready to work with; others require more groundwork before meaningful planning can begin.

Five questions to assess your readiness

1. Complexity — how many moving parts?
Pensions old and new, ISAs, property, business ownership, protection policies, mortgages, trusts, inheritance. The more moving parts, the more likely you need Level 2 or 3 integrated advice.
2. Documentation — is everything up to date?
Any adviser must understand what you hold, where it is, what it costs, and what terms apply. Missing paperwork doesn't prevent advice — but it slows the process and adds cost.
3. Behaviour — how do you react to money?
Your ability to stay disciplined during volatility, follow a plan, and avoid emotional decisions all influence the type of support you may need. People who struggle with emotional decisions often benefit from ongoing advice.
4. Property vs investments — are you clear?
No adviser group sits naturally above both property and market investing. Understanding your comfort with leverage, liquidity, rental risk, and growth helps determine whether you need specialist property advice, investment-led advice, or a broader planning approach.
5. Life transitions — are you facing a change?
Retirement, a business sale, inheritance, marriage or divorce, career changes — when life changes, financial complexity usually follows. This is where Level 2 or 3 planning becomes far more valuable than one-off advice.
Chapter 5

The key components of a financial plan

Financial advice isn't a single product. It's a combination of components — some essential, some optional, some dependent on your life stage or financial complexity. Your plan should include only the components that genuinely support your life — nothing more, nothing less.

#ComponentTypeWhat it covers
1Cashflow ModellingCoreLong-term projections; "Will we have enough?"; stress-testing life scenarios
2Investment StrategyCoreRisk level, asset allocation, portfolio design, cost structure
3Tax PlanningCoreISAs, pensions, VCT/EIS, CGT exemptions, IHT, business wrappers
4Retirement PlanningLife-stageSustainable income, drawdown strategy, annuity decisions, sequencing risk
5Protection PlanningImportantLife cover, income protection, critical illness, business continuity
6Property StrategyOften essentialHold/sell decisions, BTL viability, leverage impact, liquidity
7Business-Owner PlanningSpecialistExit strategy, remuneration, shareholder arrangements, post-exit structure
8Estate & IntergenerationalValuableWills, IHT, gifting, family investment decisions
9Ongoing Review & CoachingHigh valueAccountability, volatility discipline, plan adjustments, life changes
10Professional CoordinationDependentAccountants, solicitors, mortgage advisers, trustees
Chapter 6

How good financial advice is delivered

No matter which advice type you choose, good financial advice follows a structured, transparent process. The depth depends on scope — but the core steps are the same. Understanding this gives you a benchmark for assessing any firm: not by reputation or promises, but by the quality and completeness of their advice journey.

  • 1. Discovery — Understanding your goals, priorities, concerns, and decision-making style before discussing products or portfolios
  • 2. Data Gathering — Collecting accurate information on pensions, investments, property, protection, income, spending, and tax
  • 3. Analysis & Modelling — Assessing your situation and testing assumptions through appropriate scenario analysis
  • 4. Strategy Design — Creating a coherent, evidence-based plan aligned with your objectives and constraints
  • 5. Recommendations — Presenting clear, transparent advice with explanations, alternatives, risks, costs, and rationale
  • 6. Implementation — Executing the agreed actions efficiently and accurately, with appropriate coordination
  • 7. Ongoing Review — Keeping the plan relevant as life, legislation, markets, or circumstances change
  • 8. Communication Standards — Clear response times, reporting, review frequency, and day-to-day points of contact
  • 9. Professional Coordination — Alignment with accountants, solicitors, mortgage advisers, or trustees as needed
Chapter 7

How advisers add value — and where they don't

Adviser value comes in two forms: financial value — measurable in pounds through tax savings, better net returns, and avoiding costly mistakes — and life value — peace of mind, confidence about the future, reduced anxiety, and freedom from admin. Both are real. Both are supported by evidence.

The headline numbers

£47,706
Average extra wealth for those who received financial advice vs those who didn't, over a decade
ILC–Royal London, 2019
1.2%
Annual gap between fund returns and actual investor returns (the behaviour gap)
Morningstar Mind the Gap, 2025
~3%
Net annual value added by advisers through specific behaviours: coaching, tax, rebalancing, withdrawal strategy
Vanguard Adviser's Alpha

Where advisers genuinely add value

1. Behavioural coaching — the largest value driver
Adds value
Keeping you invested, calm, and consistent during volatile markets. This behaviour gap typically costs investors 1–2% per year. Where they don't: predicting markets, calling tops and bottoms, or promising returns.
2. Tax structuring and asset location
Adds value
Using tax wrappers efficiently, structuring withdrawals, managing allowances. Where they don't: guaranteeing tax outcomes or providing specialised tax advice beyond their regulatory remit.
3. Portfolio construction & rebalancing
Adds value
Systematic, evidence-based rebalancing. Where they don't: trying to beat the market through stock picking or timing.
4. Withdrawal strategy
Adds value
Prioritising which accounts to draw from, minimising tax drag, managing sequencing risk. Where they don't: promising specific income levels regardless of market performance.
5. Estate & intergenerational planning
Adds value
Structuring assets sensibly, identifying IHT exposure, integrating wills and trusts. Where they don't: writing wills or drafting trusts — that's a solicitor's job.
6. Clarity & confidence
Adds value
Reassurance, structure, accountability, confidence they won't run out of money. When we ask long-standing clients what they value most, the answer is rarely investment returns — it's sleeping better, fewer arguments about money, and confident decisions.

Five myths that some advisers still push

❌
Myth 1: "We can consistently beat the market." There is no evidence that retail advisers can repeatedly outperform markets. The real value is in closing the retail underperformance gap and ensuring you capture market-level returns consistently.
❌
Myth 2: "Our portfolios are unique." Most advisers use variations of the same evidence-based investment principles. The real differentiator is process, planning, and behavioural support.
❌
Myth 3: "We can predict what the market will do." Short-term prediction is statistically impossible. Good advisers focus on discipline, not forecasts.
❌
Myth 4: "Our fees pay for superior performance." Fees should be aligned with complexity, service, and planning depth — not justified by performance claims no one can guarantee.
❌
Myth 5: "We cover everything." Advisers cannot legally write wills, draft trusts, provide detailed tax advice, or manage property portfolios. A good adviser is honest about their limit of competence and introduces specialists where needed.

The wellbeing evidence

Royal London's "Feeling the Benefit" study found that 63% of people who received financial advice felt financially secure and stable, compared with 48% of those who had not. Advised customers felt up to three times more confident in their financial decisions. Aegon's research found that 44% of people with an ongoing adviser relationship combined healthy finances with a positive money mindset — compared with just 10% of people who had never used any financial advice.

When people with more than £300,000 in investable assets were asked why they use a financial planner, more than half said the primary benefit was peace of mind — the knowledge that someone competent was watching over their financial life.
